responsibility: TestDayTools: AI-assisted drafting, illustration maintenance and comparison with the official sources below. This is not a driving-instructor assessment or a study of learning outcomes.
scope: Checked the consistency of the 31 shared illustrations and labels, the eight classroom illustrations and answer-key mapping, and the three linked contrast lessons. Simplified pictures teach recognition, not sign manufacturing specifications or every state's traffic law.
corrections: The classroom school sign now uses the shared five-sided artwork. Do Not Enter lettering stays on its red background; the Keep Right arrow no longer crosses its lettering. Lane Ends retains two lane-boundary strokes without a merge arrow, and Slippery When Wet retains a vehicle and two skid tracks. The classroom pack and web reference now use the same exported sign pictures.

sources.label: New York DMV: Road Signs You Must Know

lessons.title: Stop vs. Yield: an empty road does not make the signs interchangeable
lessons.scene: Imagine two quiet approaches to an intersection. One has a STOP sign; the other has a YIELD sign. You cannot see another vehicle yet. The important difference is the control at your approach, not your first impression that the road is empty.
lessons.cue: The red octagon requires a complete stop. The downward triangle requires giving way: slow, look for road users with priority, and stop when necessary.
lessons.decision: At STOP, finish the stop before deciding whether the gap is safe. At YIELD, do not assume that slowing has given you priority. Check for pedestrians and conflicting traffic before proceeding.
lessons.mistake: If the junction looks clear, I can roll through either sign.
lessons.reason: An apparently empty junction does not cancel a STOP requirement. It also does not prove a YIELD entrance is clear: a pedestrian or a vehicle outside your first glance can still have priority. Neither sign grants permission to enter an unsafe gap.
lessons.transfer: Now a pedestrian appears as you approach the YIELD sign. Explain why stopping can be necessary even though YIELD does not require a fixed stop on every approach.
lessons.explanation: The decision changes with the conflict. You must give the pedestrian the right of way, which can require a stop. Do not memorize a number of seconds or the shortcut 'yield means never stop'.

lessons.title: Do Not Enter vs. Wrong Way: prevent the entry, then recognize a direction error
lessons.scene: You are looking for an entrance. At the mouth of one roadway you see DO NOT ENTER. Farther along a one-way roadway or ramp, a WRONG WAY sign can warn someone who has already entered in the wrong direction. This is a teaching sequence, not a placement plan.
lessons.cue: DO NOT ENTER controls entry from your direction. WRONG WAY warns that your direction of travel is wrong. Both relate to avoiding opposing traffic; neither is a general parking or speed sign.
lessons.decision: Do not enter past the first sign while searching for confirmation. If you encounter WRONG WAY after a turn, do not continue against traffic; correct the situation only in a safe, legal way. A practice illustration cannot select that maneuver for a real roadway.
lessons.mistake: I can continue until I see WRONG WAY, or make an immediate U-turn wherever that sign appears.
lessons.reason: Waiting for the second warning defeats the entry restriction. An abrupt reversal can create another conflict or be illegal at that location. Recognize the direction problem without turning the lesson into a blanket instruction to perform a particular maneuver.
lessons.transfer: Suppose the DO NOT ENTER picture is partly obscured but you can recognize its red circle and white horizontal bar. Explain why a missing second warning would not make that entry permitted.
lessons.explanation: The entry control stands on its own. WRONG WAY is another warning, not a condition that must be met before DO NOT ENTER applies. Always use the actual roadway controls and the official handbook for real driving decisions.
lessons.sourceSections: Regulatory Signs: DO NOT ENTER and WRONG WAY

lessons.title: Merge vs. Lane Ends: joining traffic is not the same as losing a lane
lessons.scene: Compare an entrance ramp joining a roadway with a two-lane section that narrows to one lane. Both situations need observation and space management. Only the second tells you that an existing travel lane ends ahead.
lessons.cue: A merge warning draws attention to joining traffic. A lane-ends warning draws attention to a lane reduction. Read the actual diagram and road markings to determine which side is affected; the simplified picture here is not a rule that the same side always ends.
lessons.decision: Look ahead and manage speed and space for the actual conflict. Do not assume the adjacent driver will stop for you. Follow the posted controls, markings and applicable local merging rules rather than memorizing one universal merge point.
lessons.mistake: Both yellow signs mean my lane ends, so I must immediately move sideways.
lessons.reason: The color identifies a warning, not the exact geometry. Joining traffic can require attention without removing your lane. A lane reduction requires preparing for the indicated change, not a sudden move without checking whether there is a safe gap.
lessons.transfer: Imagine the sign is before a ramp, but the entering traffic gets its own added lane. What extra information would you need before calling it a merge conflict?
lessons.explanation: Check the sign's specific symbol, the lane markings and the roadway ahead. A nearby ramp alone does not prove that two streams must immediately share one lane. Compare the official manual's Added Lane example with its Merging Traffic and Lane Ends examples.
lessons.sourceSections: Warning Signs: MERGING TRAFFIC, ADDED LANE and LANE ENDS; NY must-know chart
